title: Playbook: stream-safe declarative hydrator for typed Python SDK responses
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
This ticket delivers a developer-facing playbook and reference implementation for a 'declarative hydrator' layer in the Python SDK that: (1) converts streaming LLM responses into typed models (dataclasses and pydantic), (2) supports incremental/partial parsing during backpressure, (3) is idempotent across retries, and (4) manages schema evolution with clear fallback mappings.

Problem statement:
Current Python SDK helpers focus on synchronous parse-and-return flows or heavyweight deserialization that can't tolerate mid-stream interruptions. Customers building long-running streamed generation consumers need:
- deterministic hydration even when we resume from a checkpoint after a retry or connection drop,
- low-latency partial hydration for UI streaming (render tokens ASAP),
- safe schema evolution (older clients can still parse newer fields) without runtime exceptions,
- ergonomic APIs for authors to declare expected response shapes.

Goals:
- Provide a declarative way to register typed model schemas and per-field fallback/transform rules.
- Offer a streaming-aware hydrator that emits partial typed fragments and final object when stream completes.
- Ensure idempotency: rehydrating from the same checkpoint yields identical objects.
- Provide migration helpers (compatibility layer) when response contracts change.
- Ship tests, e2e example app, and migration guide for customers.

Non-goals:
- Replace user-level business validators. Hydrator focuses on structural parsing and safe defaults.
- Support every 3rd-party validation library beyond dataclasses and pydantic in v1.

Design sketch (high level):
1) Declarative schema registry: users declare a 'HydratedSchema' via python decorator or small DSL linking model classes to stream fragments and conversion hooks. Example: register a pydantic model with an 'id' key and optional 'delta' field mapping.
2) Stream event model: low-level stream events (token, chunk_json, chunk_text, checkpoint, stream_end). Hydrator consumes events and maintains a checkpoint token for resumption.
3) Incremental parser: safe, incremental JSON accumulator that tolerates partial chunks and attempts field-level extraction as data arrives.
4) Idempotent checkpointing: checkpoint tokens include a monotonic stream cursor + fingerprint of parsed fragments. Replays use fingerprinted patches to avoid double-applying deltas.
5) Schema evolution: register a migration map between versions (rename, migrate types, provide default). Hydrator applies compatible migrations automatically.

Public API sketch (Python):
```
from rw.sdk.hydrator import Hydrator, schema
from dataclasses import dataclass

@schema(version='1.2')
@dataclass
class StreamedSummary:
    id: str
    tokens: list[str]
    score: float | None = None

h = Hydrator.for_schema(StreamedSummary, on_partial=lambda s: render_partial(s))
# inside stream consumer loop:
#   h.feed(event)  # event may be 'token', 'chunk_json', 'checkpoint', 'end'
#   for obj in h.emitted():
#       handle(obj)
```
Behavior notes:
- on_partial is called with incremental typed fragments (dataclass or pydantic model) for low-latency rendering.
- final object is emitted only once at stream_end with deterministic aggregation.

Idempotent replay example: when a client restarts from checkpoint C123, Hydrator.fetch_resume_state(C123) returns a small patch list already applied; Hydrator.apply_resume avoids re-applying token deltas by tracking per-field fingerprints.

Compatibility and migration:
- Provide a CLI tool 'rw-hydrator-migrate' that generates a migration shim from v1 -> v2 for common patterns (rename field, wrap into union).

Testing and acceptance criteria:
- Unit tests: incremental parse, partial emit, final object correctness, fingerprint idempotency.
- Integration: e2e example with streaming chat UI that shows partial tokens turning into hydrated message objects.
- Backpressure test: consumer pauses for 500ms mid-stream; hydrator must preserve partial state and resume correctly.
- Migration tests: old client can parse new server responses when only additive changes introduced.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Playbook+Hydrator+Design
- Proto example app: https://github.com/redwood-inference/examples/stream-hydration
- Draft PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/1234
- Test coverage dashboard: https://dash.redwood.ai/tests/ENG-903451

Rollout plan:
1) Merge internal refactor PR behind feature flag 'hydrator_v2'.
2) Run canary with internal teams and 'beta' SDK users (open invite).
3) Collect telemetry: partial-emit latency, resume-success-rate, hydration-errors-per-1k.
4) Flip flag after 2 weeks with <0.1% error regression.

Migration instructions for customers:
- Add decorator '@schema' to their models and call Hydrator.for_schema(...) instead of manual JSON parsing.
- Use 'rw-hydrator-migrate' to generate a shim if server has breaking renames.

Risks and mitigations:
- Incorrect fingerprinting could lead to missing deltas: mitigate with conservative fingerprinting and a safe rehydrate fallback that replays raw tokens when inconsistencies detected.
- Performance overhead: keep incremental parser in pure C-free Python fast path; optional C-extension can be provided later if needed.

Open decisions (short):
- exact checkpoint token shape (opaque token vs structured cursor): prefer opaque to make internal optimizations easier.
- whether hydrator should persist checkpoints to disk: v1 will keep in-memory and expose hooks for user persistence.

Next steps (this ticket):
- Finalize schema decorator signature and emitted event model (by 2026-02-17).
- Complete core incremental parser and unit tests (by 2026-03-03).
- Integrate with Python SDK streaming API and add sample app (by 2026-03-15).
- Submit PR, collect reviews, ship behind feature flag.
